newsitem.title: USA: Moody's sees US debt concerns, but affirms at Aaa.
newsitem.headline: Moody's sees US debt concerns, but affirms at Aaa.

text.p: Moody's Investors Service Inc Thursday issued its first in-depth report on the United States and affirmed the country's triple-A credit rating.

The U.S. credit rating agency said the report was part of its effort to monitor how the United States and other developed countries intend to contend with growing healthcare and pension costs associated with an aging population.
Despite some credit concerns, the U.S. government debt rating is "still solidly Aaa," Moody's said.

"You've got these massive demographic shifts, where you are going to have increasing healthcare costs (and) increasing pension costs," Vincent Truglia, managing director of Moody's sovereign risk group, told Reuters in an interview.
Compared to Europe and Japan, however, the U.S. is in a much better economic position to fend off the pension and healthcare bulge that is likely to occur, Truglia said.

The actual level of U.S. government debt to Gross Domestic Product (GDP), adjusted for internal holdings, is about 50 percent of GDP, which is generally lower than most developed European countries, he added.
Moody's produced its report in response to increased investor demand for in-depth analysis on G-5 nations.

Unlike the 1996 congressional debt-ceiling debate that prompted Moody's to place some $300 billion of U.S. Treasury bonds under review for possible downgrade, current credit concerns do not warrant any similar action, Truglia said.
"In that particular case ... it was quite clear it was not a solvency problem," he said.
Moody's confirmed the U.S. government's Aaa rating when the 1996 Congressional debate was concluded.

Robin Monro-Davies, managing director at IBCA, the European credit rating agency, said his firm also confirmed the triple-A rating on U.S. debt immediately following last year's debt-ceiling resolution.

"Our view is that Congress is unlikely to use that route again," he said. "There are no issues, as a far as the U.S. is concerned, which make us feel anything other than that the rating is a strong triple-A," said Monro-Davies.
"Most people view Treasury debt as the highest quality available," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
U.S. Treasury debt is viewed as "the risk-free instrument in the global financial markets," he said.
